chapter: Queens Terrace, Decca records and Amen
title: Willard Brown, Buster Smith and arrangements
summary: Brown's drinking and saxophone playing, then Buster Smith's arranging and Charlie Parker's regard for him.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: (Side A of Tape 4 begins at this point.)

Buster Smith, we've got to figure out where--you would have gotten Buster--Buster was playing with Eddie Durham, when Eddie Durham had that big band up in Bridgeport in 1940, Buster was in his band and Buster and Eddie were doing that job that summer. You must have gotten Buster not long after that.
Where did Willard Brown go, to New York?
Willard Brown was drinking quite a bit.
He was a hell of a saxophone player.
He was one of the greatest things I ever had in my whole life.
He was on that tape with Frank Galbraith; he was one of the greatest.
It's funny, I would not have thought of him as being a drinking kind of guy.
Oh, he was a drinker, but he was very peaceful. The only thing he wanted to do was brag about how much he could play, and he could.

That guy could really play, because I remember his wife telling me that when he was with Benny Carter's band, they kept screaming for him, because he was playing baritone then, he could play up a storm on baritone; I heard him play and he could play like hell. I'm surprised that he didn't get better known. So, in other words, you got Buster to take his place?
Buster was another one who could play like mad.
Buster is the guy, the only guy that Charlie Parker looked up to. I know
a guy asked him, who is the best saxophone, Buster Smith, the greatest in the world. But he was so unassuming and just a wonderful guy, it was such a relief that he didn't drink, very quiet.

No. He could arrange like mad, he made a lot of arrangments for me. I got a thing in there--the last arrangement I made for my band, for my six piece band at the Queens Terrace, Way Down Upon the Swanee, I got it right in there on a 78 we took. To hear what we were doing and how I was writing then, I had a lot of ambition, a lot of pretty girls to look at at the Queens Terrace, and they were--oh, lord, I couldn't get off the bandstand. I sure had a lot of fun.
